lines: A coal miner brought a canary down into the mine.
If poison gas came, the bird would collapse first.
Deadly gas could build up in coal mines. Miners called it damp.
White damp was air with carbon monoxide, toxic even at low levels.
After damp, left by explosions, carried carbon monoxide too.
In 1907, 3,242 American coal miners died. It was the worst year ever.
In 1895, a scientist named John Scott Haldane had an idea.
Put a warm-blooded animal in the mine to detect carbon monoxide.
A canary breathes fast, it's small, and it burns energy quickly.
So the poison hit the bird before it hit the men.
When the canary showed distress or collapsed, the miners got out.
You see, it's like a smoke alarm with feathers.
It goes off before you notice anything.
In 1914, American experts tested small animals with carbon monoxide.
Canaries were the best for the job.
And unlike mice or guinea pigs, canaries recovered quickly in fresh air.
Britain, the United States and Canada all used them, well into the twentieth century.
Today, a canary in the coal mine means anyone who warns us of danger first.

claims.claim: Coal miners brought canaries into coal mines as an early-warning signal for toxic gases, primarily carbon monoxide.

Build-ups of hazardous gas in mines are known as damps; white damp is air containing carbon monoxide, toxic even at low concentrations; after damp forms after an explosion and contains carbon monoxide.
3,242 U.S. coal miners died in 1907, the worst year ever.
John Scott Haldane proposed placing a warm-blooded animal in a mine to detect carbon monoxide in 1895; canaries were used as early as 1896.
The bird's rapid breathing, small size and high metabolism made it succumb before the miners, giving them time to act.
Canaries in distress or collapsing let coal workers evacuate; a 1914 report found canaries best adapted and, unlike mice or guinea pigs, they recover quickly in fresh air.
Britain, the United States and Canada used canaries well into the 20th century; 'canary in the coal mine' is now an idiom for a warning of danger.
